title: Raw Material Risk Threatens Europe’s Drone Race
content:
Europe’s race to develop drones is an urgent feature of discussions around the continent’s defense policy and investment. This year, venture capital funding for European defense start-ups is projected to quadruple to €10.5bn ($11.8bn), with about three-quarters going to drone development and manufacturing.

The scale and pace of this build-out is spurring demand for materials. Key among these are a set of critical minerals, including gallium for semiconductors, germanium for optics, rare-earth elements for brushless motors, and cobalt and graphite for batteries, which are all crucial in drone production.

While drones may only use these minerals in small or even trace quantities, sourcing is a challenge as supply chains are often murky, concentrated, and at risk of disruption.

Extraction is only part of the problem. While more than 60% of cobalt, which is widely used in batteries essential for powering drones, is extracted from the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Copperbelt, for example, more than 70% of world supply is refined in China.

title: NATO Must Prepare for Russian Missile Swarms
content:
Low-cost Russian cruise missiles are the latest evolution of the Russian airborne threat. They are substantially cheaper than the higher-end legacy cruise missiles and, at the same time, they are more powerful and lethal than the masses of long-range drones Russia has so far relied on for saturation strikes.

As a result, Russia has found a new cost-effective, mass-produced tool to overwhelm Ukraine’s air defenses and pummel its critical infrastructure. It would be wrong, however, to assume that these missiles challenge only Ukraine. In a direct confrontation with Russia, European NATO states would be equally ill-prepared.

Russia’s shift from long-range drones to low-cost cruise missiles began with Geran-3. The Geran-3 was functionally very similar to the Geran-2 long-range drone but replaced its piston engine with a JT80 turbojet produced by the Chinese manufacturer Telefly. This roughly doubled the system’s speed from 185 kph to 350 kph (115 mph to 214 mph) and raised its cruising altitude from 4,000 meters to 7,000 meters (13,000 ft. to 23,000 ft.), allowing it to escape existing Ukrainian long-range drone defenses.

title: Russian Strikes Rise Across NATO’s Eastern Flank
content:
There have been at least 17 attacks on NATO’s frontline states and Moldova in the past month, either with proven or suspected Russian direction.

The alliance’s political leaders and military commanders now face a deteriorating picture, with some member states on the Black Sea making urgent appeals for military support, including combat aircraft and anti-drone systems.

Russia’s campaign still uses so-called sub-threshold attacks that are provocative and damaging, even lethal, while remaining just short of triggering NATO’s Article 5 common defense. But Russia’s behavior is becoming more reckless, as with the attempt to destroy aircraft at Leipzig airport in August and attacks on merchant shipping (detailed below). The pattern is also notable for attacks on Elon Musk’s Starlink system, seen as critical to the operations of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

Here are some of the most recent incidents:

Poland. September 23: Starlink terminal outside Warsaw set on fire. Polish government says Russian involvement likely.

Moldova. October 3: Three Russian missiles and two drones entered Moldovan airspace. Debris found on Moldovan soil.
snippet: There have been at least 17 attacks on NATO’s frontline states and Moldova in the past month, either with proven or suspected Russian direction.

title: It’s the Networks, Stupid
content:
It took Reform leader Nigel Farage less than 12 hours following Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s maiden speech at September’s UN General Assembly to falsely claim the UK’s new National Centre for Information Defence (NCID) would be a “Ministry of Truth to clamp down on free speech.”

Given that the scope and powers of NCID have yet to be determined, Farage’s comments had no evidential basis.

Burnham spoke of a center that would “detect, attribute and disrupt” hostile state attacks and an organization that would “support and defend our democracy.” The prime minister and officials who have worked on this announcement and will shape the eventual center should be congratulated on this move and supported in their efforts.

The “chiefs” tasked with shaping the center now have decisions to make in terms of the scope, scale, and priorities of NCID.

What are the key considerations?

Firstly, NCID will not decide what Britons are allowed to say. Genuine speech of any kind, along with domestic information manipulation activity (DIM), should not be within its scope.

title: Deepening Black Sea Crisis Demands US Involvement
content:
Something very serious is happening in the Black Sea, and it demands a response. Merchant ships are being attacked and sunk without warning in the latest, highly provocative action in Russia’s shadow war against European NATO members.

A slew of drone attacks on merchant vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, attributed to Russia, have killed at least two sailors and left 21 missing. On October 5, a Turkish cargo ship hit by drones sank in Romania’s exclusive economic zone. The following week, two chemical tankers were set ablaze, one just inside and one just outside Romanian territorial waters. A total of seven ships have been hit. Romania responded on October 17 by shooting down two drones identified as jet-powered Russian Geran 4s, which were headed westward toward the country.

Some of the vessels were engaged in trade with Ukraine, but several were not, suggesting that the Kremlin’s attacks served a wider and more worrying purpose.

title: Changing Ukraine’s President Will Change Nothing
content:
Donald Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Vladimir Putin agrees, as does Elon Musk, and the point was once made by that great friend of Ukraine, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. So, let’s imagine that, somehow, fair and free elections with no Russian interference were to be held tomorrow in Ukraine. Who would win?

According to a September 23 public opinion survey conducted by a respected polling outfit, the winner would either be Ukraine’s incumbent president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, with 23% or Gen. Valery Zaluzhny, the former commander in chief of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, with 22.9%. Former President Petro Poroshenko comes in third with 10.7%. Fourth place goes to Zelenskyy’s intelligence aide, Kyrylo Budanov, with 9.5%, while fifth goes to the far-right politician and commander of the 3rd Army Corps of the Ukrainian Ground Forces, Andrii Biletsky, with 8.7%. Other polls show similar results.

title: Will Serbia’s Vote End the Vučić Era?
content:
Almost two years of protests against corruption and incompetence in Vučić’s government may have forced his hand, but calling an early election (scheduled for October 25) is a trick he has successfully used before. He is gambling on his opponents struggling to convert their support on the streets into comparable success at the ballot box.

It is the first time in Serbia’s multiparty era that the National Assembly has been dissolved at the same time as the president resigning, and as the lead candidate for his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Vučić aims to return as prime minister. The constitution won’t allow him to run for president a third time.

Snap parliamentary elections in Serbia have occurred so often that they are something of a national tradition. Since 1992, Serbia has held just three scheduled parliamentary elections, compared to 10 snap votes.

Such unscheduled elections have helped Vučić overcome political difficulties before, including unpopular reforms in 2016, the consequences of an opposition boycott in 2022, and protests over the government response to two mass shootings in May 2023.

title: Dodging Russian Drones on Europe’s Highway to Hell
content:
Europe’s longest road, the E-40, begins its 5,000-mile journey at the port of Calais, long the gateway to the British Isles, and ends in the Altai Mountains of Kazakhstan.

It’s part of the E-road system, which aims to help unite Europe in trade and to aid development and ties between neighbors; until 2014, it was doing just that. Now, when you drive about 2,000 miles along the route, you come upon strange and otherworldly sights signaling your arrival at a battlefield, the key sector for Ukraine’s desperate fight to repel the Russian invader.

This summer I drove twice from the UK to the fortress belt with volunteers delivering aid to the defenders.

We entered the Channel Tunnel at Folkestone and emerged in Calais to take the E-40 across France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, and Ukraine all the way to a crossroads at Slovyansk where the road becomes impassable as it peels off toward Russian-occupied Bakhmut.

Going right at that crossroads leads 13 miles to Kramatorsk, and then it’s 22 miles further to Kostyantynivka, another battlefield frustrating Putin’s plans.
snippet: Europe’s longest road, the E-40, begins its 5,000-mile journey at the port of Calais, long the gateway to the British Isles, and ends in the Altai Mountains of Kazakhstan.
creator: Sara George

title: Republicans and Democrats Agree on AI Reform
content:
Artificial intelligence has moved center stage in the upcoming midterm elections, propelled by a backlash against data centers and fears about AI safety. In response, Congress vows to act.

Democratic and Republican Members of Congress opened CEPA’s annual Tech & Security Conference with a rare sign of consensus: AI safety and innovation are not contradictory, insisted Representative Nathaniel Moran (R-TX-01). He compared the need for regulation to the rules that forced automobile companies to make cars safe.

“The brakes allow you to drive faster, not slower,” said Moran. “AI brakes should not slow innovation. They should enable faster movement with a safe backstop.”

This is the logic behind Moran’s proposed AI Kill Switch Act. Co-sponsored with Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu, it would require developers of the most powerful frontier AI models to be able to throttle, suspend, or completely shut models down if they threaten $100 million in economic damages or 10 deaths.
snippet: Artificial intelligence has moved center stage in the upcoming midterm elections, propelled by a backlash against data centers and fears about AI safety. In response, Congress vows to act.
creator: Bill Echikson

title: Russia Restocks its Hostage Bank
content:
The main Russian security service, the FSB, arrested a foreign reporter on suspicion of espionage — this time a journalist for the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun in the Far Eastern Sakhalin region.

The incident is the latest addition to what some journalists-in-exile refer to as the Kremlin’s exchange fund. Others in the West term it a hostage bank of Westerners visiting Russia who are plucked by the FSB as a means to apply duress on their governments.

Thirty-four-year-old Yuki Imai looked bewildered and shocked as several masked FSB operatives stormed his hotel room in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the Pacific island of Sakhalin in Russia’s Far East, and threw him half-naked onto the floor. The FSB brazenly advertised its visible brutality with a video showing his arrest.

The Japanese journalist was then put on a plane bound for Moscow, and upon landing immediately taken to a Moscow court, which ruled that he should be sent to Lefortovo — the notorious FSB prison — and kept in a cell until December 12.

title: Could China and Russia Rescue Cuba’s Regime?
content:
The energy blockade has become the principal instrument of pressure employed by Washington against the Cuban regime. Unlike other coercive measures, restrictions on hydrocarbons directly affect the country’s ability to function and have resulted in repeated and lengthy nationwide power cuts.

The strategy became particularly significant after the overthrow and capture of Nicolás Maduro in January, which enabled the US to disrupt oil shipments from Venezuela, one of the principal sources of support for Cuba’s economy. Washington also put pressure on Mexico, which had become an increasingly important energy supplier to the island.

President Donald Trump’s January 29 executive order, which established a mechanism for imposing additional tariffs on countries supplying oil to Cuba, joined together sanctions on key sectors of the Cuban economy in a strategy intended to increase the costs of sustaining the communist regime from abroad.

But the effectiveness of the blockade depends on Washington’s ability to deter other states from providing Havana with the resources it needs.
